children: A prolonged global oil supply shock has forced iCapital to pull up its year-end target range for the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield
to 4.5%–5.3%, as the Federal Reserve is embarking on its first rate-hiking cycle since 2022–2023.

range by 25 basis points to 3.75%–4.00%, joining the European Central Bank and Bank of Japan in tightening monetary policy. iCapital expects the U.S. central bank to raise rates at both remaining meetings this year—October and December—unless global oil supply meaningfully recovers by mid-November in the wake of the Middle East war.
Markets are already pricing in another hike by year-end and two more by the end of 2027.

Beyond the immediate energy crisis, iCapital pointed to structural forces keeping rates elevated for the long term. The reversal of multi-decade globalization trends has fundamentally changed the economic calculus: "Efficiency was the organizing principle of the old system. Resilience is the organizing principle of the new one, and resilience costs more," it said in a blog post.
Compounding matters, iCapital said, U.S. federal debt has surpassed $40T, with mandatory spending, net interest, and defense accounting for more than 85% of government expenditures.

Geopolitical flashpoints remain the critical variable. Middle East supply bottlenecks—including disruptions at the Strait of Hormuz and Houthi control of Red Sea access—have pushed U.S. gasoline prices above $4 per gallon and diesel above $6 per gallon. The correlation between oil
prices and interest rates has never been higher, making energy
markets the dominant factor in determining where yields finish the year, according to iCapital.

title: iCapital raises rate outlook as Fed launches new hiking cycle
